tldr: Instead of collecting massive task-specific motion-capture data, this work cleverly combines generic locomotion data with ordinary tennis videos to achieve a reactive control policy that lets a real humanoid robot rally with human players.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the ATHLETE framework. Reference motions are synthesized from videos and locomotion data using Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM). It then trains a timing-adaptive teacher policy, distills it into a student policy, and fine-tunes it via task reinforcement learning (PPO), ultimately yielding a real-robot policy that operates without reference motions.
overview:
When trying to get humanoid robots to play intense sports like tennis, the biggest bottleneck is the cost of collecting training data. The combinations of incoming ball positions, timings, and the approach motions needed to reach them are endless. Covering all of them with human motion capture is simply impractical.

The authors noticed that when humans learn a new sport, they combine their existing walking and running experience with demonstrated swing motions. Instead of collecting tennis-specific whole-body motions from scratch, their idea is that an open-source generic locomotion dataset (LAFAN1) and just about 10 minutes of ordinary tennis practice video should be enough.

In the proposed framework ATHLETE, Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) combines trajectory optimization and motion matching to automatically generate diverse reference motions that naturally bridge locomotion and striking. Next, it trains a teacher policy that can freely stretch or compress striking timing, and transfers privileged reference information to a student policy via online distillation (DAgger). Finally, by fine-tuning with task rewards and physical domain randomization, it produces a reactive policy that directly drives the whole body from ball and robot states without looking at any reference motions at deployment.

Experiments on a real humanoid robot recorded high hit success rates of 90.00% on forehands and 86.67% on backhands. It also achieved multi-shot rallies (up to 8 shots) with both amateur and professional tennis players, proving that dynamic whole-body interaction skills can be acquired from low-cost data sources.
contributions: Proposing Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to automatically synthesize diverse tennis reference motions by combining public locomotion data with ordinary monocular tennis videos.
Training a time-adaptive teacher policy that flexibly alters playback speed to match striking deadlines, enabling matching with a wider range of incoming balls.

Distilling privileged reference motion information via latent representation alignment and DAgger to realize a reactive control policy that requires no reference motions or online planning during real-robot deployment.
Achieving a 90.00% forehand and 86.67% backhand hit rate on a real humanoid robot, enabling multi-shot rallies with human players.

sections.heading: Can humanoids learn tennis without dedicated mocap?
sections.summary: Tennis requires fast locomotion, precise whole-body impact, and adaptation to rapid changes, but collecting dedicated motion data covering diverse approaches and contact locations is extremely costly. This study proposes ATHLETE, a framework that solves this challenge by synthesizing existing generic locomotion data with sparse video-derived striking motions.
sections.details:
When teaching dynamic tasks like tennis to humanoid robots, the biggest obstacle is data coverage. The incoming ball position, speed, and arrival time differ every single time. Training a whole-body policy that handles all of this requires combinations of varied approach locomotion and striking forms, but capturing all of them with motion capture is prohibitively expensive.

Prior studies have attempted to use human motion data as prior knowledge, but the difficulty of gathering dedicated data covering the vast combinations from approach to impact remained. On the other hand, high-quality generic locomotion datasets like LAFAN1 already exist, and tennis striking forms can be extracted from regular practice videos on platforms like YouTube. In other words, locomotion experience and striking skills can be sourced separately.

The core idea of ATHLETE is to treat these two heterogeneous data sources as complementary and synthesize the necessary whole-body motions itself. By smoothly connecting approaches and swings via trajectory planning and motion matching, it builds a set of reference motions covering diverse contact points. Furthermore, by combining supervised learning and reinforcement learning, the goal is to ultimately obtain a controller that does not rely on reference motions, but immediately reacts with the whole body upon seeing the ball trajectory.

(a) shows the striking height distribution for forehand and backhand, and (b) shows the contact position distribution on the XY plane in the robot local frame. While the original data in orange clusters near the front, the generated data in cyan spreads widely around the robot.

sections.heading: Where does it stand in motion generation and whole-body control?
sections.summary: This section reviews related work on motion data generation for humanoids and reinforcement learning-based whole-body control. ATHLETE sets itself apart from existing hierarchical planning methods by synthesizing motions via trajectory optimization and motion matching while ultimately condensing everything into a single reactive policy.
sections.details:
### II-A Data Generation for Humanoids
Motion Matching—a technique developed in gaming and animation that searches a database for frames with the closest pose and trajectory features to stitch them smoothly—has recently seen growing robotics applications. Examples include work combining basic skills and locomotion in parkour. Generative models synthesizing motions from text or history are also active. However, ATHLETE uses planar trajectory optimization to strictly solve the approach path, satisfying geometric constraints for contact and transition, and then applies tracking correction via physics simulation.

### II-B Humanoid Whole-Body Control
Imitation learning tracking human reference motions is a dominant approach for humanoid whole-body movements. Prior work targeting tennis includes LATENT and AdaPT. LATENT learned a modifiable action space from imperfect motion primitives, and AdaPT combined video-derived motions with hierarchical planners for speed-adaptive tracking.

However, these prior works often required high-level planners or reference motion selection mechanisms during execution, introducing latency and system complexity. ATHLETE incorporates the task-goal-driven reward design of TaskNPoint while designing a time-stretchable teacher policy, and critically differs by distilling it into a single reactive policy that takes no reference motion inputs at all.

sections.heading: The TGMM pipeline: Beautifully connecting locomotion and swings
sections.summary: Combining 16 LAFAN1 walking sequences with 164 swing clips reconstructed from a 10-minute video, TGMM synthesizes diverse whole-body reference motions. It calculates approach paths via trajectory optimization to stitch locomotion, and corrects discrepancies using a mimic policy in physics simulation.
sections.details:
### III-A Material Preparation and Impact Matching
The source materials comprise 16 locomotion motions from the LAFAN1 dataset and 164 swing motions (67 backhand, 97 forehand) extracted from a 10-minute tennis practice video. Skeletal poses are recovered from video using GVHMR, and retargeted to the robot via GMR.

As the first step of synthesis, a random target contact point $\mathbf{b}$ is sampled around the robot. It selects forehand or backhand based on lateral ball position, and computes a geometric cost (Eq. 1) between the target position and the contact point $\mathbf{c}_i$ of each candidate clip. With higher weight on height discrepancies, it selects the swing clip with the lowest cost.

### III-B Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM)
Next, it plans a path for the robot to naturally walk to the start position of the selected swing. When the distance $d$ is short ($d \le 1.5\,\mathrm{m}$), translation while maintaining heading dominates; for longer distances, it switches between running while turning toward the travel direction and realigning its heading right before the hit.

Based on these planar dynamics, it solves for a minimum-time, smooth-control trajectory via nonlinear optimization using CasADi and IPOPT (Eq. 2). From the resulting trajectory, future positions and velocities are extracted as a feature query $\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathrm{query}}$, and a global search finds the best matching frames from the LAFAN1 walking library to stitch together (Eq. 3). This builds a whole-body approach motion with seamless footwork and approach.

### III-C Composition and Dynamic Correction
At the transition from locomotion to swing, the frame with the closest features is selected as the entry frame, and offset inertial blending (Eq. 4) removes discontinuities in joint and root positions.

However, purely geometric blending leaves physical joint limit violations and inertial inconsistencies. To fix this, a mimic policy based on BeyondMimic is trained to track the reference motion inside a physics simulator. The resulting physically feasible rollout trajectories are recollected, completing the dynamically corrected reference motion dataset used for training in the next section.

captions.F3: Illustration of striking motion generation via TGMM. The yellow sphere is the target contact point, and the blue line shows the optimized planar root trajectory. The translucent blue robot represents the locomotion phase, green represents the swing phase, and the green curve traces the racket sweet spot.

sections.heading: Three-stage learning: Time stretching, policy distillation, and task fine-tuning
sections.summary: Using the synthesized reference motions, it first trains a time-adaptive teacher that adjusts striking deadlines. Next, it matches motions with simulated ball trajectories, distills them into a student policy via online DAgger to eliminate reference motion inputs, and finally pushes striking quality to the limit with PPO.
sections.details:
### IV-A Stage 1: Time-Adaptive Teacher Policy
Standard imitation learning fixes motion playback speed, making it unable to handle variations in incoming ball speed. Therefore, a teacher policy is trained via PPO to stretch or compress the same reference motion to fit different striking deadlines.

For a nominal duration $\bar{T}_i$, target deadlines $T_i$ are sampled from $[\bar{T}_i/2, \bar{T}_i]$. The teacher policy outputs not only joint torque commands $\mathbf{a}_t$ but also phase acceleration $\ddot{\phi}_t$. This allows it to speed up or slow down motion progress as needed to precisely hit a static ball at the specified time. Thanks to this mechanism, a single motion clip can be paired with balls at diverse velocities.

### IV-B Stage 2: Ball Trajectory Matching and Student Policy Distillation
Balls are launched in simulation from various positions and velocities, and post-bounce trajectories are matched with reference motion contact points both spatially and temporally within Stage 1 deadlines (using 200 reference motions).

Next, knowledge from the frozen teacher policy is transferred to the student policy deployed on the real robot. Here, DAgger (Dataset Aggregation: interactive imitation learning where the expert labels states visited by the student) is adopted to prevent distribution shift. Even more crucial is the latent representation design. It provides a privileged encoder $E_T$ that observes future reference motion sequences, and a student encoder $E_S$ that takes only a 5-step history of robot and ball observations. Imposing an alignment loss (Eq. 6) to bring the student latent $\mathbf{z}_t^S$ close to the privileged $\mathbf{z}_t^T$ enables the student to self-infer striking intent and timing from observation history alone.

### IV-C Stage 3: Task Refinement via PPO
The distilled student policy masters striking basics, but falls short of returning balls accurately into the opponent's court. Therefore, the encoder is frozen, and only the policy head and value network are fine-tuned via PPO.

The reward incorporates racket velocity direction at impact $f_{\mathrm{swing}}$, outbound ball speed toward the opponent court $f_{\mathrm{out}}$, net clearance $f_{\mathrm{net}}$, and target landing accuracy $f_{\mathrm{land}}$. To bridge the Sim-to-Real gap, ball mass, restitution coefficient, drag, and racket inertial properties are heavily randomized across environments (domain randomization). This training results in a fully autonomous reactive policy running at 50Hz, needing neither reference motions nor phase control during real-robot deployment.

captions.F4: Overall three-stage learning flow of ATHLETE. It seamlessly connects (1) data generation and dynamic correction, (2) time-adaptive teacher training, (3) privileged representation alignment and student distillation via DAgger, (4) PPO task refinement under randomized physics, and (5) real humanoid deployment in a motion-capture environment.

sections.heading: Achieving a 90% hit rate and rallies with humans on the real robot
sections.summary: After verifying the coverage expansion achieved by TGMM, striking performance was evaluated in simulation and on the real robot. In real-robot experiments, hit rates reached 90.00% for forehand and 86.67% for backhand, successfully sustaining rallies of up to 8 shots with human players.
sections.details:
### V-A Coverage Evaluation of Reference Motions
First, the coverage of incoming balls achievable by the TGMM-generated library was tested. Across 10,000 ball trajectories at the same library size (164 motions) and $K=1$ candidate, the original motion library matched only $7.57\%$, whereas the TGMM-generated motions reached a $42.64\%$ success rate (Fig. 5). Expanding to 200 motions reached $99.21\%$ at $K=8$, proving that even a compact library can accommodate diverse balls.

### V-B Striking Accuracy in Simulation
Testing the time-adaptive capability of the teacher policy yielded physical contact in 493 out of 500 trials ($98.6\%$), with a mean absolute timing error of $71.23\,\mathrm{ms}$ relative to target deadlines (Fig. 6).
Furthermore, an ablation comparing policy performance with and without Stage 3 fine-tuning (PPO) revealed a decisive gap. The distilled policy alone without fine-tuning achieved hit rates of only $1.26\%$ (forehand) and $5.67\%$ (backhand) and failed to clear the net. With PPO fine-tuning, hit rates dramatically surged to $94.97\%\, /\, 95.04\%$, and return rates (clearing the net) reached $91.19\%\, /\, 92.20\%$. Sweet-spot error was also cut in half, from around $14\,\mathrm{cm}$ to about $6\,\mathrm{cm}$.

### V-C Real-Robot Experiments and Benchmarks
Using a Unitree humanoid, balls and robot base poses were tracked via external mocap, controlled at 50Hz from a PC equipped with an RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU. In hand-tossed tests of 30 balls each, the robot achieved hit rates of $27/30$ ($90.00\%$) for forehand and $26/30$ ($86.67\%$) for backhand. Net clearance rates were $46.67\%$ and $53.33\%$, respectively.
It showed hit and return rates comparable to or better than the prior method AdaPT. In rally experiments with humans, it sustained rallies of up to 5 shots with a novice player and up to 8 shots with a professional player (Fig. 7).

Compared to the original 164 motions (orange), the TGMM-generated 164 motions (blue) and 200 motions (green) achieve substantially higher matching rates, demonstrating markedly improved spatial and temporal coverage.
captions.F6: Distribution of contact timing errors for the teacher policy across target deadline ratios $\alpha$. Across 493 physical impacts, 72.4% fall within ±50ms of the target deadline (cyan band), demonstrating precise timing adjustment with a mean error of 71.23ms.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: ATHLETE demonstrated that dynamic tennis skills can be learned from generic locomotion data and sparse videos. A reactive policy running without reference motions achieved high hit rates on the real robot and multi-shot rallies with humans. Future challenges include ball perception with onboard cameras and acquiring diverse playing styles.
sections.details:
Inspired by how humans combine existing motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, this work established ATHLETE, a framework that realizes humanoid tennis without expensive tennis-specific motion capture.

Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) geometrically and dynamically aligns heterogeneous data. Through distillation from a time-adaptive teacher and reinforcement learning fine-tuning, the framework ultimately elevates this into a reactive whole-body controller that requires no reference motion inputs at all. High hit rates and human rallying capabilities shown in real-robot experiments confirm that this is a powerful approach balancing data efficiency with ease of deployment.

However, the current system relies on external motion capture for ball state estimation. As future work, the authors highlight transitioning to visual feedback via the robot's onboard cameras, and exploring learning methods that maintain diverse shot types and play styles rather than collapsing into a single striking behavior.

takeaways: Even with a low-cost mix of 'generic locomotion data' and 'isolated swings from video', trajectory optimization acts as a bridge to automatically synthesize high-quality whole-body motions.
Having the teacher policy output 'phase acceleration (time progression speed)' flexibly stretches or compresses clip playback speed, enabling it to handle balls with widely varying speeds.

Compacting privileged reference motion information into observation history via latent representation alignment and DAgger distillation completely eliminates the need for online motion planning or reference tracking at deployment.
Because the distilled policy alone lacks sufficient contact accuracy, PPO fine-tuning in a physics simulator with domain randomization is the deciding factor for Sim-to-Real success.
limitations: Complete reliance on an external motion-capture system to estimate 3D ball positions, velocities, and the robot base pose (not yet operational with onboard cameras alone).
During PPO task fine-tuning, some of the diverse human-like swing styles originally extracted from videos tend to collapse into a single efficient striking motion.
Simulation conditions are restricted for the physical environment, such as capping return ball speeds to fit the constraints of the test area (a compact mocap area of roughly 10.5m x 5.5m).
